transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-09-02 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Jorge Martinez (Nimbus CTO), Priya Singh (Nimbus ML Eng), Amir Haddad (Nimbus Ops)

Summary:
High-level POC scoping discussing success criteria, workload sizing, benchmark plan, and decision criteria between hosted, dedicated, and private deployment modes. Customer is latency-sensitive retail search/recommendation service with strict data residency and KMS requirements; timeline aims for internal decision within 4 weeks.

Topics:
- Success criteria: p95 latency, throughput, cost per inference, result quality
- Workload sizing: QPS, sequence length distribution, concurrency patterns
- Benchmarks: synthetic vs production replay, dataset, metrics, monitoring
- Deployment modes: tradeoffs Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem)
- Security/compliance: SOC2, audit logs, KMS, SSO, RBAC

Action items (captured above).

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Hi everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros from our side — I'm Samira, AE, and Liam's our solutions engineer.
[00:07] Liam: Hey all, hi. I'll be driving the technical bits today.
[00:10] Jorge: Jorge here, CTO at Nimbus. Priya and Amir are with me. We're trying to scope a POC to validate latency and cost for a retail re-rank stage.
[00:20] Priya: hi, thanks. Our high level: we have a re-ranker that sits between retrieval and final ranking. We see spiky QPS around marketing campaigns, typical sequences ~50-120 tokens, sometimes up to 400 for longer context. Latency target is p95 < 120ms for the re-ranker.
[00:40] Amir: We're also strict about data residency and want to ensure customer PII never leaves our VPC — or if it does, it's encrypted with a key we control.
[00:50] Samira: Great — that gives good framing. If we frame success criteria as p95 < 120ms, accuracy delta < 1% vs your baseline, and cost per 1M requests under a threshold, we can design a POC to validate those. Are those ok?
[01:05] Jorge: Yes. Also need to know what tradeoffs there are across hosted, dedicated, and private. Cost and ops burden matter.
[01:15] Liam: Sure — short summary: Hosted is quickest to start, managed by Redwood, good for most customers with predictable SLAs; Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and slightly better tail latencies; Private (VPC or on-prem) gives the strongest isolation and customer-controlled keys/networking but increases deployment time and ops responsibility.
[01:35] Priya: For the re-ranker we care mostly about latency, predictability under burst, and data control. How much does dedicated improve p95 vs hosted typically?
[01:45] Liam: It depends on workload and model. With dedicated reserved capacity you avoid noisy neighbors and can tune batching aggressions. In our experience for similar re-ranker workloads, dedicated can shave 10–30% off p95 compared to multi-tenant hosted when under heavy load, and it lets you pin specific GPU types and quantization profiles. But it comes with a commit cost.
[02:05] Jorge: And private? If we'd want KMS keys in our account and VPC-only access, is that supported?
[02:12] Samira: Yes — Private supports customer-managed KMS and VPC peering or a private endpoint. On-prem goes further but requires more integration work. We also have audit logs and SOC2 docs we can share.
[02:25] Amir: Good. For the POC we'd probably want to run two benchmark windows: one against hosted and one against dedicated — to compare p95 and cost. If private is chosen later, we'd scope separately.
[02:38] Liam: That makes sense. For the benchmark we typically ask for: a) representative payloads (token lengths, prompt templates), b) target QPS patterns (sustained and burst), c) eval set for quality checks. We'll provide a script to replay traffic and collect latency/throughput, token counts, and model outputs for A/B quality comparison.
[02:55] Priya: We can provide a week of anonymized logs and the eval set. Sequence lengths vary; median ~75, 90th ~180. Bursts up to 400 RPS for a few minutes during campaigns.
[03:10] Liam: Good — that helps size capacity. For those numbers, we typically recommend starting the dedicated sizing conversation around X GPUs (we'll compute exact numbers after an initial run) — we can estimate based on model, batching window, and acceptable latency.
[03:25] Jorge: Speaking of models, we're looking at a 7B re-ranker right now. Any quantization advice?
[03:33] Liam: 7B models often quantize well to 4-bit or 8-bit depending on the model family. Quantization reduces memory and can improve throughput; we have tested quantized variants in both hosted and dedicated contexts. The main caveat is small quality regressions; we'll include an eval to measure delta.
[03:50] Samira: On the decision criteria piece — many customers do a two-step: quick hosted POC to validate quality and baseline latency, then dedicated POC to validate sustained performance and cost. Private is usually last if they need KMS-in-customer-account or on-prem constraints.
[04:08] Priya: That matches what we'd expect. Timeline — we need senior leadership buy-in in ~4 weeks. Can we run hosted baseline in one week and dedicated benchmark the following?
[04:18] Samira: Yes, hosted baseline can be spun up within 48–72 hours once we have the data and API keys. Dedicated benchmark requires capacity reservations or a trial dedicated pool; we'd aim for 1–2 weeks lead time.
[04:30] Amir: Network: we need to understand egress patterns and whether Redwood supports private endpoints. Also KMS — we want keys in our AWS account, HSM-backed if possible.
[04:42] Liam: We support customer-managed KMS integration for Private; for Dedicated we can also integrate keys depending on contract. We have private endpoints and VPC peering options for Private. For Hosted, keys are managed by Redwood by default but we have bring-your-own-key options for enterprise customers under Dedicated/Private. I'll follow up with the exact network topology docs.
[04:58] Jorge: Compliance: can you share SOC2 and ISO attestations and the audit log format?
[05:04] Samira: Absolutely — we'll include SOC2/ISO reports and a sample audit log schema in the packet.
[05:10] Priya: Benchmarks — what metrics will you capture? We care about p50/p95/p99 latency, tail CPU/GPU utilization, tokens/sec, batching statistics, and quality metrics (NDCG or rank correlation) vs our baseline.
[05:22] Liam: We'll capture all of those: latency percentiles, per-request token counts, model throughput, batch sizes, KV cache hit rates if used, and we'll produce a CSV with outputs for quality evaluation. We'll also include cost modeling (estimated tokens/requests per month x unit costs).
[05:38] Jorge: Cost modeling is key for leadership. We'll want to see cost per 1M requests for hosted vs dedicated, and reserved vs on-demand for dedicated.
[05:48] Samira: We'll provide a clear cost comparison. For Dedicated we'll show committed vs usage-based scenarios. For Private, there will be onboarding and infra cost plus a license/fee.
[05:58] Amir: For security we need SSO/SAML and RBAC for role separation. Is that standard?
[06:05] Liam: Yes — SAML SSO and role-based access controls are standard for Dedicated/Private and available for Hosted enterprise accounts. Audit logs and session traces are available as export.
[06:16] Priya: A couple of technical details: do you support prefix/KV caching to reduce repeated context costs? We have a lot of repeated prefixes for product descriptions and combos.
[06:25] Liam: Yes — Redwood supports KV/prefix caching and automatic prefix deduping in the runtime. That will reduce token counts and latency for repeated prefixes; we'll enable it in the benchmark and measure cache hit rates.
[06:36] Samira: Ok let's outline the POC plan: Step 1 (Host): run hosted baseline with sampled traffic replay + quality eval to validate accuracy and baseline latency (1 week). Step 2 (Dedicated): reserve capacity and run dedicated benchmark to validate p95 under burst and cost tradeoffs (1–2 weeks). Optional Step 3 (Private): only if needed for KMS/VPC/on-prem — separate project.
[06:58] Jorge: That sounds reasonable. In terms of acceptance criteria — if hosted meets p95 < 120ms and quality delta < 1% we could potentially stay hosted, but if p95 drifts during campaign bursts or cost is too high, we'd push to dedicated.
[07:15] Priya: And what about fallbacks? We want graceful degradation — fall back to a smaller model or async queue if we hit capacity.
[07:24] Liam: Redwood supports routing policies and fallbacks — you can route to a cheaper variant or degrade to lower-cost model under high load, or use an async queue for non-critical requests. We'll capture that in the ops runbook.
[07:36] Amir: For benchmarking we need to know what hardware you plan to use for dedicated tests — A100, H100, or older?
[07:45] Liam: We can run dedicated on a few GPU types; we'll propose H100 for the strictest latency tests and A100 for cost-optimized runs. We'll specify exact instance types in the benchmark plan.
[07:56] Jorge: Also interested in quantization + calibration steps — will you run quantized model quality checks?
[08:02] Liam: Yes, we'll run FP16 and int8/4-bit variants where supported and surface the quality delta. We'll include an automated eval run to produce NDCG/precision metrics.
[08:12] Samira: Any blockers on your side to get started?
[08:15] Priya: We'll need an NDA signed and a place to drop anonymized logs. Also a short security questionnaire answered.
[08:23] Samira: We can get the NDA and security doc pack over by EOD tomorrow. We'll attach the SOC2 and network/topology docs.
[08:30] Amir: Good. On the network front, we'll need a whitepaper showing how VPC peering or private endpoints are configured and whether Redwood supports strict egress controls.
[08:39] Liam: I'll include the network whitepaper and a sample terraform/ansible snippet for peering.
[08:44] Jorge: Decision criteria recap — quality, p95, cost, and security/integration effort. Leadership will weigh cost vs speed to production.
[08:53] Samira: Great — so immediate next steps: Samira will send the pricing/comparison and NDA; Liam will send benchmark plan and infra checklist; Nimbus will share sample payloads. Then we'll schedule the hosted baseline.
[09:05] Priya: For the benchmark script, can we have an option to simulate campaign bursts (400 RPS for 5 minutes) and also sustained 50 RPS?
[09:12] Liam: Yes — we'll parameterize the script for sustained and burst patterns and include ramp-up/ramp-down behavior.
[09:18] Amir: One more ops question: does Redwood provide per-token cost breakdown and a dashboard for token-level costs?
[09:24] Samira: Yes — Redwood Console surfaces token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route/model and you can export reports. We'll include screenshots in the packet.
[09:34] Jorge: Competitors — we evaluated Anthropic and Bedrock. Bedrock felt like less mature in terms of per-token cost visibility; Anthropic had different model tradeoffs. We're open to Redwood if the POC shows clear latency/cost advantage.
[09:50] Samira: Understood. We'll make sure the benchmark compares apples-to-apples and include a cost model.
[09:56] Liam: Quick note on instrumentation — we'll need distributed tracing hooks or at least a way to correlate request IDs so you can join your logs with our benchmark traces.
[10:05] Priya: We'll add a request id header in the replay.
[10:09] Samira: Perfect. Anything else?
[10:12] Jorge: No, that's it for scope. Thanks.
[10:15] Samira: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the packet and proposed calendar for the benchmark.

End of transcript.
